w: What's tested How insulin works (C-peptide, GLUT4, the insulin receptor, potassium) and where each drug acts Types of diabetes, its complications, drugs that raise glucose, and diagnosis by A1C and glucose The insulin preparations: rapid, short, intermediate, long and ultra-long, and which to use when Every non-insulin class with examples: mechanism, adverse effects, contraindications and key pharmacokinetics Comparing the drugs for a situation: hypoglycemia, weight, heart failure, kidney function Dental relevance and treating hypoglycemia in the chair Dr. Pius Fasinu (Pharmacology) taught this two-hour lecture on Tuesday, November 3. He opened by calling diabetes the biggest topic in endocrinology, one that takes a very big chunk of every exam, and he judged every drug by the same few questions: does it cause hypoglycemia, does it cause weight gain, and which patient should get it. He finished by working through the practice questions at the end of his slides. "If you need to know anything at all in endocrinology, diabetes is the one that you want to know." And: "In the exams, diabetes takes a very big chunk of assessment." Why it matters, including in the dental chair The CDC's newest numbers count about 40.1 million Americans with diabetes, about 1 in 8. Many more have prediabetes, and about 80 percent of them don't know it. Diabetes-related care took about a quarter of health-care spending. Because diabetes has few symptoms early, the real number is probably higher, and many people first learn they have it from an eye exam or a dental visit. The slide lists the dental relevance: a higher risk and greater severity of periodontal disease, delayed wound healing, more oral infections, xerostomia and its complications, and hypoglycemia during dental procedures. The optometry side is diabetic retinopathy, diabetic macular edema, cataracts, fluctuating refractive errors and other vision-threatening retinal complications. "It might be the optometrist, it might also be the dentist, right? So you have to look out for those things... you have to blend all of those things together in your study." What diabetes is Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders whose common feature is hyperglycemia, caused by defects in insulin secretion, in insulin action, or most commonly both. He stressed that hyperglycemia is a feature, not the disease: pregnancy, other illnesses and many drugs can raise glucose too. In older patients, most diabetes comes from both problems at once: they don't make enough insulin, and their tissues don't respond well to what they make. Diabetes is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease, of adult-onset blindness, and of non-traumatic lower-extremity amputation. The amputations come from neuropathy and delayed wound healing: a patient who can't feel a foot wound doesn't notice it, it becomes infected, gangrene sets in, and amputation is the only solution left. Insulin: secretion, synthesis and C-peptide When glucose is low, the pancreas releases glucagon, which breaks down glycogen and raises plasma glucose. When glucose is high, it releases insulin, which moves glucose out of the blood and stores it as glycogen in the liver and muscle. Insulin secretion is stimulated by glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and ketone bodies, and by the incretin effect: insulin secretion is greater after oral glucose than after the same glucose given intravenously, because the gut adds its own signal. Beta cells make insulin as proinsulin, which is cleaved into insulin (the A and B chains) plus C-peptide, the piece that held the chains together. The two are made in equal, or equimolar, amounts. That makes C-peptide a test. An insulin level can't tell injected insulin from the patient's own, but injected insulin carries no C-peptide. So in someone who has injected insulin for years, an absent C-peptide means the pancreas has stopped making insulin. This matters because, with time, a person with type 2 diabetes can stop making insulin, as in type 1. "C-peptide level will always tell you if they are making insulin at all, or if they are not making." Glucose transporters and the insulin receptor Glucose enters cells through membrane transporters called GLUTs. Only one matters for diabetes treatment: GLUT4, the insulin-dependent transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue. GLUT1, 2, 3 and 5 work without insulin. GLUT1, for example, handles basal glucose uptake and carries glucose across the blood-brain barrier, because the brain can't wait for insulin. The insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase that spans the membrane. Insulin binds its outer part, the receptor phosphorylates itself, and the signal runs through insulin receptor substrate, then PI3 kinase, then Akt (protein kinase B). The key result is GLUT4 translocation: GLUT4 sits inside the cell in the cytoplasm, and insulin's signal moves it into the membrane so glucose can enter. Skeletal muscle More glucose uptake (GLUT4), glycogen synthesis and protein synthesis Liver Less gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; more glycogen synthesis and lipogenesis Adipose tissue More glucose uptake (GLUT4) and triglyceride storage; less lipolysis Potassium More uptake into cells through Na/K-ATPase The last row is worth knowing. Potassium is held tightly between about 3.5 and 5, because both low and high potassium cause arrhythmias, tremor and muscle weakness. Because insulin drives potassium into cells, insulin is one of the best ways to bring down a high potassium, even in people without diabetes. It is given together with glucose, so that insulin has glucose to clear and the patient doesn't become hypoglycemic. Symptoms and complications The classic symptoms are polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia, with weight loss and blurred vision. They are often mild or absent, and the disease may be present for years before it is diagnosed; getting up at night to urinate is often the first thing people notice. Acute complications: diabetic ketoacidosis, when cells lack glucose and the body burns fatty acids into ketone bodies, and the non-ketotic hyperosmolar state, driven by the sheer amount of glucose in the blood, which can lead to stupor, coma and death. The hyperosmolar state carries the higher mortality of the two. Chronic complications are split by vessel size. Microvascular: neuropathy, nephropathy and retinopathy. Macrovascular: coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease and stroke. "Micro is the one that involves neuropathy, nephropathy, and retinopathy. Those three are very important to know." Types of diabetes Type 1: absolute insulin deficiency, usually from autoimmune destruction of the beta cells (or a pancreas that was removed). The patient can't make insulin and depends on injected insulin. Type 2: peripheral resistance to insulin plus an inadequate secretory response. There is insulin, but the tissues don't respond well to it. Prediabetes: glucose higher than normal but not yet diabetes, with a high risk of progressing. It has no symptoms, but it is not a given that it becomes diabetes: diet, lifestyle change and weight loss can reverse it. Secondary diabetes: gestational diabetes; diseases such as acromegaly, Cushing syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, chronic pancreatitis and cancer; and drugs. Secondary means there is a primary cause, and you treat the underlying cause, not the diabetes. Antipsychotics Alter receptor binding, increasing insulin resistance Beta-blockers Inhibit insulin secretion Corticosteroids Peripheral insulin resistance plus gluconeogenesis Fluoroquinolones Act on insulin secretion through the beta cell's ATP-sensitive potassium channels Protease inhibitors Block the conversion of proinsulin to insulin Thiazide diuretics Inhibit insulin secretion through hypokalemia A1C and diagnosis Glucose binds hemoglobin covalently, forming glycosylated hemoglobin; HbA1c is hemoglobin A with a sugar attached to its first amino acid. The higher the blood glucose, the higher the percentage of hemoglobin glycated. Because the bond is irreversible, the A1C doesn't come down when glucose falls; it reflects glucose over the red cell's life span of about 3 to 4 months (90 to 120 days). An A1C of 8 or 9 percent means glucose has been high, on average, for months. Diagnosis used to need high glucose on two separate visits, the way blood pressure is diagnosed. Now a single blood draw can confirm diabetes, because the A1C and a fasting glucose come from the same sample. You need two agreeing results: HbA1c Below 5.7% 5.7 to 6.4% 6.5% or higher Fasting glucose Below 100 mg/dL 100 to 125 mg/dL 126 mg/dL or higher 2-hour oral glucose tolerance Below 200 mg/dL with a working pancreas Not given in class 200 mg/dL or higher Random glucose Unreliable alone Not given in class Above 200 mg/dL So an A1C of 6.5 percent or higher, a fasting glucose of 126 milligrams per deciliter or higher, a 2-hour glucose tolerance value of 200 or higher, or a random glucose above 200. Prediabetes is an A1C of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or a fasting glucose of 100 to 125. A random glucose isn't very reliable on its own, because it depends on when the person last ate. "We have four parameters here, and you need two to be able to diagnose." Treating type 1 diabetes: insulin Type 1 is simple to treat: the patient can't make insulin, so you give insulin. What you need to know is the types of insulin, how they are used, and their side effects. The professor said dose calculations in units won't be needed. Human insulin comes as regular (R), sold as Humulin R and Novolin R, and NPH. There are also six analogs of human insulin: the rapid lispro, aspart and glulisine, and the long glargine, detemir and degludec. Before recombinant insulin, pig (porcine) insulin, which differs from human insulin by one amino acid, was used for decades; it has now essentially left the market. NPH stands for neutral protamine Hagedorn: neutral because the solution is neither acidic nor basic, protamine because that protein slows the insulin's absorption from the injection site, and Hagedorn after the researcher. It was the first change made to lengthen insulin's action, so patients could inject fewer times a day. Rapid-acting (analogs) Lispro (Humalog), aspart (NovoLog), glulisine (Apidra) Onset 5 to 15 minutes; lasts about 4 hours Mealtime (bolus), as needed Inhaled, very rapid Afrezza Acts within 1 to 2 minutes Mealtime Short-acting (regular, human) Humulin R, Novolin R Peaks about 3 hours; gone by about 8 hours Before meals; no prescription needed Intermediate (NPH, human) Humulin N, Novolin N Onset 2 to 4 hours; protamine slows absorption Longer coverage; no prescription needed Long-acting (analogs) Glargine (Lantus, Basaglar), detemir (Levemir) Slow, steady release, no real peak; glargine lasts more than 24 hours Basal, once daily Ultra-long Degludec (Tresiba); glargine as Toujeo Degludec lasts more than 42 hours Basal Treatment is basal-bolus. The basal insulin, for example glargine injected once at night, lasts more than 24 hours and mimics the body's own background insulin, whether or not the patient eats. The bolus is a rapid-acting insulin taken as needed (PRN) before each meal to cover the post-meal spike; skip the meal, skip the bolus. Patients learn to match the bolus to the size of the meal. Two of these, regular and NPH, are sold without a prescription, from the pharmacist the way Sudafed is sold, to patients who know how to use them. Only these two. "It's common to have questions that ask you, someone is planning to eat something, and what type of insulin they need." For a meal about to be eaten, NPH is too slow: its onset is 2 to 4 hours. In his practice question the choices were regular, NPH and glargine, and his answer was regular, the fastest of those three; the rapid analogs are faster still. Adverse effects of insulin: hypoglycemia, the main one and the watchword for every drug that raises insulin release; weight gain, because insulin is anabolic; transient deterioration of retinopathy, a temporary worsening of eye disease when insulin is started; and lipoatrophy or lipohypertrophy at the injection site. The non-insulin drugs These are mostly used for type 2 diabetes. They used to be called oral hypoglycemic agents, but that name no longer fits, because several are now injected. The classes: insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas and meglitinides), the biguanide metformin, thiazolidinediones, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, the incretin drugs (GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors), the amylin agonist pramlintide, SGLT2 inhibitors, and two others, the bile acid sequestrant colesevelam and the dopamine agonist bromocriptine. Know the mechanism of each and at least a couple of examples. Insulin secretagogues: sulfonylureas and meglitinides Secretagogues make the pancreas secrete insulin. A sulfonylurea binds the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) on the beta cell's ATP-sensitive potassium channel and closes it. Potassium is trapped, the membrane depolarizes, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and the calcium influx causes exocytosis of insulin the cell has already made. This stimulation is continuous, whatever the glucose level. Two consequences follow. First, secretagogues only work in a patient whose pancreas can still make insulin: if beta cells have stopped, it doesn't matter how much you stimulate them. Second, they share insulin's side effects: hypoglycemia and weight gain. They also have low durability: after a year or two the dose has to go up, and eventually they stop working, because there is a limit to how far the pancreas can be squeezed. Other adverse effects are agranulocytosis, jaundice, nausea and vomiting, and hypersensitivity, since some people react to sulfur drugs. Warnings: G6PD deficiency, where the drug can break down red cells; liver disease; kidney disease, mostly glyburide; and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, the same warning as metronidazole, so patients should avoid alcoholic drinks. The first-generation chlorpropamide (Diabinese) is long-acting with a high risk of hypoglycemia and is rarely used. The second generation is more potent and shorter-acting: glyburide (Diabeta, Micronase, Glynase), glipizide (Glucotrol) and glimepiride (Amaryl). Meglitinides, repaglinide (Prandin) and nateglinide (Starlix), work on the same channel: they share two binding sites with the sulfonylureas and have one of their own. They are rapidly absorbed, peak in about 1 hour and have a half-life of about 1 hour, so they are dosed with meals to target the post-meal spike, a quick squeeze on the pancreas (Prandin is named for postprandial). They cause hypoglycemia, though less than sulfonylureas, weight gain and low durability, need frequent dosing, and shouldn't be used if a sulfonylurea has failed. "Any drug that works by stimulating insulin release will have this same side effect of hypoglycemia." Metformin, the first-line drug Metformin is the only biguanide worth knowing, and it is still the first-line drug for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in an otherwise healthy patient. Comorbidities can change that: a patient with a weight problem may start on a GLP-1 agonist, and a patient with heart failure or cardiovascular disease may start on an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 agonist. Its exact mechanism isn't clear, so focus on its effects. Its primary effect is to inhibit hepatic gluconeogenesis. It also increases peripheral insulin sensitivity, especially in skeletal muscle, and it delays glucose absorption from the gut, which turns a big post-meal spike into a slow plateau. The net effect: less glucose made by the liver, less absorbed from the gut, and better insulin sensitivity. Crucially, metformin has no effect in normoglycemic states. Insulin and the secretagogues lower glucose whatever it is; metformin won't bring a normal glucose lower. So its risk of hypoglycemia is very low, and it is weight neutral or causes modest weight loss. Adverse effects: GI upset (nausea and vomiting, indigestion, cramps, bloating, diarrhea), which usually fades in one or two weeks; decreased vitamin B12 absorption, so some patients need B12 injections monthly or every 3 months; and lactic acidosis. Contraindications: an eGFR below 30, which is absolute, and acute or chronic metabolic acidosis. Cautions: excessive alcohol, unstable or acute heart failure, and hepatic impairment. When metformin is no longer enough after a few years, other drugs are added on. "If it's normal, metformin will not bring it lower." And on the kidneys: "When the GFR is less than 30, we do not give them metformin." Thiazolidinediones Pioglitazone (Actos) and rosiglitazone (Avandia) are PPAR-gamma agonists. PPAR-gamma is a nuclear receptor, mostly in adipose tissue, that switches on genes of glucose and lipid metabolism. The result is more fat cells and fat mass, more fatty acid uptake into fat, and better insulin sensitivity in muscle and liver. Their signature problem is edema, which is dose-related, with weight gain and new or worsened heart failure, since peripheral and pulmonary edema are what heart failure looks like. They are contraindicated in NYHA class III or IV heart failure, and are now recommended only for patients without cardiovascular problems. They also raise the risk of macular edema; the professor said he skipped it in class, but it is on the slide. Avoid them when ALT is more than 2.5 times the upper limit of normal. Advantages: a low risk of hypoglycemia, preserved beta-cell function, higher HDL, and lower triglycerides and blood pressure. Incretins: GLP-1 receptor agonists The two incretins, GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide 1) and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide), are released from the gut in proportion to the nutrient load. GLP-1 receptors are on beta cells and in the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidney, lung and gut. GLP-1 increases insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent way, decreases glucagon release, slows gastric emptying and decreases food intake. So its drugs treat hyperglycemia and cause weight loss. The body's own GLP-1 is broken down quickly by the enzyme DPP-4, so nobody saw it as a drug. Then exendin-4 was found in the saliva of the Gila monster: a potent GLP-1 agonist that DPP-4 doesn't metabolize, with a half-life of 2 to 3 hours. It became exenatide: Byetta, injected twice daily before meals, and later Bydureon, a weekly slow-release form. Today's analogs last up to a week. Exenatide Byetta; Bydureon Peak 2 hours SC twice daily before meals; Bydureon weekly From Gila monster exendin-4; renal clearance Lixisenatide Adlyxin Half-life 2 to 4 hours Once daily Proteolysis and renal Liraglutide Victoza Albumin-bound; half-life 12 to 24 hours Once daily Proteolysis Dulaglutide Trulicity Half-life 5 days Weekly Proteolysis and renal Semaglutide Ozempic (SC), Rybelsus (oral) Half-life 7 days Weekly SC, or daily by mouth Also approved for cardiovascular risk and kidney disease Tirzepatide Zepbound Half-life 5 days Weekly SC Recently approved for sleep apnea Side effects: nausea and vomiting, dose-dependent and fading with time; delayed gastric emptying, which can slow the absorption of drugs that need rapid absorption, such as oral contraceptives and antibiotics; rare pancreatitis; and acute renal failure. All carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors seen in animal studies, so people with a history of thyroid cancer are advised not to take them. Advantages: a low risk of hypoglycemia as monotherapy, weight loss and preserved beta-cell function. Disadvantages: expense, injection (with the extra cost of pen needles for daily forms), and poor tolerance in some people. Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) is the one tablet; because it is poorly absorbed, the daily oral dose is far larger than the weekly injected one. Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) is now also approved for patients with cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, and tirzepatide (Zepbound) for sleep apnea. "If somebody has a weight problem, obviously everybody here should know that GLP will be the first-line drug." DPP-4 inhibitors Instead of giving a GLP-1 drug, you can block DPP-4, the enzyme that breaks down the body's own GLP-1 and GIP, so the incretins made after each meal last longer. The gliptins, sitagliptin (Januvia), saxagliptin (Onglyza), linagliptin (Tradjenta) and alogliptin (Nesina), are all oral, once daily. Sitagliptin Januvia Reversible, competitive Renal; the exception that may be used in heart failure Saxagliptin Onglyza Covalent CYP enzymes Linagliptin Tradjenta Reversible, competitive No renal adjustment needed Alogliptin Nesina Reversible, competitive Renal Advantages: no hypoglycemia, weight neutral, well tolerated, no renal adjustment for linagliptin, and usable in kidney and liver dysfunction. Disadvantages: expense, modest A1C lowering, low durability (about 2 years), and avoid in heart failure, except sitagliptin. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors Acarbose (Precose) and miglitol (Glyset) inhibit alpha-glucosidase in the intestinal brush border, so starch, dextrin and disaccharides aren't broken down and less glucose is absorbed after a meal. They work best on a starchy, high-fiber diet with little glucose or sucrose. Acarbose is minimally absorbed; miglitol's absorption is saturable; both are cleared by the kidney. Because the carbohydrate stays in the gut, the adverse effects are malabsorption, flatulence, bloating and diarrhea, which depend on the dose and the carbohydrate eaten, plus some transaminase elevation, a sign of liver toxicity. They don't cause hypoglycemia or weight gain. They decrease the absorption of other drugs: digoxin with acarbose, propranolol and ranitidine with miglitol. They are contraindicated in bowel disorders and in liver or kidney impairment, and are not widely used anymore. Amylin and pramlintide Amylin, or islet amyloid polypeptide, is co-secreted with insulin by the beta cells. It acts on receptors in the hindbrain to decrease glucagon release, slow gastric emptying and increase satiety, and in type 2 diabetes it forms amyloid fibers. Pramlintide (Symlin) is its synthetic form, injected under the skin before meals, with a half-life of about 50 minutes and renal clearance, usable in both type 1 and type 2. Adverse effects: nausea and vomiting, and hypoglycemia when used with insulin. Few people still use it, now that the GLP-1 drugs exist. SGLT2 inhibitors Glucose is filtered at the glomerulus and then almost all of it is reabsorbed by the sodium-glucose transporter. SGLT2 inhibitors block that reabsorption, so the patient pees out the sugar: they induce glucosuria in a dose-dependent manner. They are highly selective for SGLT2 and lower glucose with rarely any hypoglycemia. The names end in -gliflozin, which, in a memory aid he passed on, sounds like flushing the sugar away. The adverse effects follow from the sugary urine and the water it pulls along (osmotic diuresis): genital fungal (yeast) infections in men and women, urinary tract infections, polyuria, and dizziness and hypotension from the lower circulating volume. Hyperkalemia is also listed: in the professor's words, when you lose sodium through these transporters, you tend to keep potassium. The warnings: fracture risk, lower bone mineral density (canagliflozin), bladder cancer (dapagliflozin), rare euglycemic DKA, acute kidney injury (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin), and a boxed warning for amputation, below the knee (canagliflozin, ertugliflozin), which was significant in clinical trials. Canagliflozin Invokana Below 45 Boxed warning for amputation; lower bone density; kidney injury; positive cardiovascular outcomes Dapagliflozin Farxiga Below 60 FDA approved to treat heart failure; bladder cancer risk; kidney injury Empagliflozin Jardiance Below 45 Indication to reduce major cardiovascular events; positive cardiovascular outcomes Ertugliflozin Steglatro Below 60 Boxed warning for amputation Bexagliflozin Brenzavvy Not given Once each morning, by mouth Advantages: hypoglycemia is rare, positive cardiovascular outcomes (empagliflozin, canagliflozin), they can be added to any other antidiabetic drug, and they lower blood pressure. Because they act as diuretics, they help heart failure too, and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) is FDA approved to treat it. "Somebody has cardiovascular problem, and naturally you give them diuretics to help them pee, and now they have a newly diagnosed diabetes. Why won't you consider something like Farxiga?" Other drugs: colesevelam and bromocriptine Colesevelam, a bile acid resin used for cholesterol, is oral and barely absorbed. Bile acid metabolism is abnormal in type 2 diabetes; its glucose-lowering mechanism isn't established, but it may decrease glucose absorption. It causes GI effects such as constipation, can raise triglycerides, and decreases the absorption of other drugs: warfarin, phenytoin, verapamil, glyburide, thyroxine, ethinyl estradiol and the fat-soluble vitamins. Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist, is the last class on the list; it wasn't discussed. He called the bile acid resins not very popular drugs for diabetes. Treating hypoglycemia Because everyone with type 1 diabetes, and many with type 2, use insulin, hypoglycemia remains the big problem, and every patient is taught to recognize the signs early. A patient who notices them can take high-sugar foods or drinks: orange juice, regular soda or glucose tablets. In an emergency, glucagon is the drug of choice, which raises glucose from the liver. It comes as a dry powder kit mixed with water for injection, a stable liquid for injection, or nasal glucagon, given the way nasal naloxone is. Comparing the drugs and choosing one The professor said it "a thousand times": when you compare diabetes drugs, ask which ones cause hypoglycemia and which cause weight gain. Insulin Yes Gain Sulfonylureas and meglitinides Yes Gain Metformin No Neutral or modest loss Thiazolidinediones No Gain GLP-1 agonists No (alone) Loss DPP-4 inhibitors No Neutral SGLT2 inhibitors Rare Not discussed Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors No No weight gain Newly diagnosed, otherwise healthy: metformin. Weight problem: a GLP-1 agonist such as semaglutide. Heart failure already on a diuretic: an SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin; avoid the TZDs, and among the DPP-4 inhibitors only sitagliptin. Cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease: semaglutide or an SGLT2 inhibitor with cardiovascular benefit. eGFR below 30: no metformin; linagliptin needs no renal adjustment. History of thyroid cancer: avoid GLP-1 agonists. "If you're going to be expecting questions, especially in your board exam, watch out for insulin, watch out for GLPs, watch out for the sodium glucose transport inhibitors... Metformin being the first-line drug." And: the questions "try to test what you choose in certain situations." Summary by target and by route More insulin secretion: sulfonylureas and meglitinides; glucose-dependent with GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors. Less hepatic glucose output: metformin (and the TZDs). Insulin sensitizers: TZDs (and metformin); the TZDs also decrease lipotoxicity. Less glucagon: GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors and the amylin analog. Slower absorption: alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists and amylin. More renal glucose excretion: SGLT2 inhibitors. One mix-up from class to know about: going through the practice question on which class raises insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent way, the answer read out was sulfonylureas. His summary slide, and his own point that sulfonylureas release insulin whatever the glucose level, say otherwise: the glucose-dependent drugs are the GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors. This hub follows the slide. By route, insulin (apart from inhaled Afrezza), pramlintide and the GLP-1 agonists (apart from oral semaglutide) are injected. Sulfonylureas, meglitinides, metformin, the TZDs, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are all taken by mouth.
